Our hon. friends opposite accuse us of always talking blue min and of decrying the principles which make for the upbuilding of a country. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that we are far from being blue ruinists. We believe in a policy which has built up another nation, and into whose markets we are now clamoring for admission. We believe in looking into the past and learning from it, and following those same principles which have built up the neighbouring republic. We are not blind to what is going on round about us. It is only a matter of common sense to determine what the future policy of this country should foe.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are now waiting to find out what the United States are going to do at the next session of congress. Why wait to see what they are going to do? Why not put into force in this country now a tariff which will provide work for Canadian workmen, build up our own factories, and make this young country a prosperous nation? When hon. gentlemen opposite have waited and have seen what the United States is going to do, are they going to come back to the House of Commons next session and say:	We cannot
do anything with regard to the tariff this year because we are waiting to see what Germany is going to do? And the following year they may be waiting to see what France is going to do. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the tariff policy of the Liberal party is to make a tariff against a foreign country, while the policy of the Conservative party is to make a tariff, not against any foreign country, but for the benefit of Canada.
The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) emphasized the word " retaliation " in connection with the tariff. He said:	Our
friends opposite are urging that we retaliate. Where in the world did he ever hear us use that word? The word "retaliation" has nothing whatever to do with the policy of the Conservative party. It is quite unnecessary; our tariff policy is not one which calls for retaliation against any foreign country. We make our tariff policy on the same principle on which the United States make theirs, and retaliation does not enter into it at all. It is my hon. friend himself who has interjected that word into the discussion. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) spoke of what the United States had agreed to at Geneva. But congress says, No, the protective principle is good enough for us; it has stood us in good stead and we will stick to it. Is there anything wrong in that? A pro-
tective policy which has been good enough for the United States in all these years of prosperity which it has enjoyed should certainly be good enough for a few more years to come. When congress meets and decides upon its tariff policy-and their ways and means committee is meeting to-day and discussing means of building up their own manufacturing, agricultural and mining industries -is there any reason why we, who are a foreign country to them, should exercise the threat of retaliation? The idea is ridiculous. These retaliatory measures which our friends opposite apparently intend to follow are the very measures which lead to international complications. Retaliation is a policy which should form no part of our national life, living as we do side by side with a friendly nation. We are supposed to be the binding link between the English-speaking nations of the world. We are a small nation with a great responsibility when we assume that role but I hope that we shall always be capable of that responsibility. We shall never maintain it, however, if my hon. friends opposite have nothing to offer to this country but a policy which calls for retaliation, and which seems a direct threat against the United States. My hon. friend from West Elgin mentioned nothing which would justify his charging hon. gentlemen on this side with being advocates of retaliation, because there is nothing in our policy, and especially in our tariff policy to suggest it.
What have we been buying from the United States? What have been our trade relations with them? Why are we on this side of the house objecting to the so-called tariff policy of hon. gentlemen opposite? I am afraid the Minister of Finance, who comes from the good old province of Quebec, must have found some difficulty in sliding over to the low tariff policy, because that is not the policy of the province of Quebec. The words " low tariff " are something new, I think, in the annals of the Liberal party from that province, and I for one am interested in	finding out	just how	low	theywill go in	their tariff	policy.	They	arepreaching low tariff this year, but next year, when they find they have to protect Canadian industry and Canadian goods, they will be the very ones to use the word " protection." And yet my hon. friends opposite say that theirs is the right policy. How long are they going to persist in this disastrous policy? How long have we to stand idly by, with our population fixed at 9,000,000, losing hundreds of thousands of our best citizens, our artisans, to the United States every year? I hope my hon. friends get a lot of satisfaction from their merriment, but it is ill timed. We as the representatives of the people of the Dominion are supposed to be legislating for their benefit, we are supposed to be building up the industries of Canada, we are supposed to be looking after the workingmen of Canada, and yet we enact legislation that tends to build up industry in the United States, apparently oblivious of the fact that the time will come when we shall be called to account for our failure to discharge our responsibilities and do something for the benefit of Canadians.
Ngiw, sir, let me turn to a different subject. This government is always telling us about the wonderful trade treaties it has negotiated with other countries. We have trade treaties with France and a dozen other nations. About the last to be negotiated was the treaty known as the West Indies Trade Agreement Act, dated July 6, 1925. Under this treaty we have entered into an agreement which will benefit the West Indies as well as Canada. We have a merchant marine with a deficit last year of about $6,000,000. One of the principle clauses of this agreement provides for the importation of bananas from the West Indies. Where are we getting our banana supplies to-day? We are giving Jamaica, Trinidad and the other West Indian islands a steamship service for which we have built several 6.000-ton ocean liners, which are provided with special refrigerator accommodation to bring bananas to our doors at a cheaper rate. But bananas are still coming into Canada duty free. No preference has been given the West Indies under this trade arrangement, and will not be given until, as the Liberal government says, " the service is com-

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
pleted." When will that service be complete? In the meantime where are we buying our bananas? We are buying them from the United States. And they do not grow bananas in the United States because that country imports them. We poor Canadians will allow American ships to bring in bananas from the very people with whom we have a trade agreement, delivering those bananas at New York or in some other American port, shipping them over American railroads to Buffalo or some other American port, and then into Canada. And we purchase them. This is taking place under the trade arrangement which this government made with the British West Indies. How do hon. gentlemen opposite explain it. Where is the benefit to Canadians? Have the Canadians paid less for bananas since the treaty went into force? Not at all. We are still buying bananas shipped from America and I presume we shall continue to buy them for several years. I cannot understand the principles underlying trade treaties that operate in this way. I should think that the Canadian government merchant marine ought to get the advantage of the freight in connection with bananas coming from Trinidad and Jamaica. As a matter of fact, this was understood when the treaty was under discussion in this house; the house understood that the treaty was being made including other things for the benefit of the banana trade in the West Indies. Read the trade agreement and you will find that accommodation is made for 70.000 bunches of bananas on every ship! But if you look at our imports from the West Indies you will find only a few dozen bunches of bananas coming up the Atlantic in some ocean greyhound bound for Canada.
As I stated in the beginning, I am a protectionist. As for the Conservative party, at the masthead of its ship of state flies the protectionist flag. It has in the past and it may again go down into the surging waters of defeat. But the ship will be raised by the wise foresight of a great people, having faith in their principles. And, sir, as the protectionist flag was the last thing to go under, it also will be the first thing to come up, flying more boldly than ever at the masthead, because of the renewed confidence of a common sense electorate believing in Canada first, last and always.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words regarding the subamendment moved on March 14 by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). That subamendment reads:

That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after "house" and substituting therefor the following:
"urges upon the government the consideration of an immediate and substantial increase of the British preference as a step towards freer trade relations between Canada and other nations."
This subamendment brings up the whole question of the British preference. The government have done nothing definite with regard to British preference, for they have on the tariff been everything by fits and starts and nothing for long and have no economic principles.
It was proposed two or three years ago to adopt a national coal policy so that every pound of coal would be mined and coked under the British flag, whether from Wales, Nova Scotia or Alberta. Such a policy would in the coal industry establish a real British preference. That was intended to implement the British preference policy and the government after a great many days adopted the resolution and then refused to carry it out. At the same time the question was discussed of affording protection to the ooal and steel industries of the maritime provinces, and for three or four years this was delayed also pending the completion of the Duncan report.
That policy was one of protection namely a system of bonuses, subventions and subsidies for the maritimes with respect to coal and steel.
But the government pooh-poohed the idea, declaring that it was not a suitable policy for this country. No; they were content to have this country send $56,000,000 a year over to Pennsylvania to help the mining industry there at the expense of the Welsh miners. The government have simply dilly-dallied with the whole problem from 1922 to the present time, and they have failed to put into effect the report of the Duncan commission, or adopt a national coal supply which would be equivalent to a British preference.
We are willing to consider what should be done to assist the motherland in a large way in order to encourage trade and industry within the empire, because trade should follow the flag; it should follow lines of national defence, Hon. gentlemen opposite have been talking a good deal about the British preference, quoting Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding as pioneers in this regard. But Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding were not the pioneers of the British preference movement; Hon. Joseph Chamberlain and Sir Charles Tupper and the 'ate Colonel George T. Denison were

The Budget-Mr. Church
the pioneers or authors of the whole movement. England to-day finds herself, a free trade country, shut out of the markets of the world. She has lost her shipbuilding orders to the Hamburg yards and she is losing her supremacy in coal, as the result of the failure of the colonies to come to her support in her hour of economic trial. After all, it is just as necesary in time of peace as it is in time of war for the country to mobilize all its resources, to keep its workmen employed, to preserve its own markets and to repel the foreign invader. It is just as necessary for Canada to mobilize in time of peace, to resist the economic invader at her door as it is for her in war to repel that invader. In war we mobilize our transportation facilities and all the natural and other resources of the country for the purposes of defence, and the same thing should apply in time of peace. What do we find in the mother country today? Thousands of men are starving in Wales and while this government can send millions to Japan and other countries to relieve distress from floods and famine, when they are asked to do something to bring relief to the Welsh miners they refuse to take action or to vote a copper. They simply make a football of the whole question; they say that they can do nothing because they have not been asked by the British government. Had this government been sincere they would have done something, sitting at the round table of the colonial conference and planning for a real British preference and cooperating with the overseas dominions, Australia and New Zealand, to work out a solution of the three major problems of the British empire defence, trade and immigration. The keynote of the empire trade problem is the extension of the British preference doctrine, bringing it up to date, and not relying upon the principle as it stood twenty or twenty-five years ago, when we had a lop-sided preference which was not a real preference at all. The British preference has been meddled with by the government, who have tried to introduce free trade piecemeal with the world at large.
We have entered into free trade arrangements with every country under the sun except such regions as Patagonia, to which the government have not as yet extended their free trade principles. Small "five, ten and fifteen cent" countries have been given preferences in our market and our tariff has been amended to give them free trade piecemeal, at the expense of the Canadian working man and in discrimination against the working man of the old land.
There are over a million and a half men out of work in England now, which shows that this present so-called British preference is of very little practical value in providing work there for our own kith and kin. If the government meant business at all, instead of saying at the last colonial conference that they were quite satisfied and had nothing at all to propose for the relief of unemployment in the old land or anything else, they would have sat around a table and done something to relieve the coal industry in Wales, for example, where there are millions of tons of coal which could be utilized in Canada to-day. The government have a merchant marine, although they sold some of the ships without public tender for $50,000; these ships could have been utilized to put the British preference into effect in a proper way in respect to coal and other products. Are we to continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the people of the United States while hundreds of thousands of our young people go to that country to live? Are we to be forever an adjunct to the United States in a trade sense? We buy from the United States every year $900,000,000 worth of high priced manufactured goods. The hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) said last night that 50 per cent of those goods could be manufactured in Canada, but in my opinion almost 70 per cent of the manufactured goods we import from the United States could be produced in this country. So I say the time has gone when the government can fool the people with their lopsided British preference and their pro-American tariff which operates against the unemployed in the old country. When we buy'goods from the United States we pay for them with our raw materials, and we cannot continue to do that much longer under such an absurd system of reciprocity. A special session of the United States congress has been called to meet this month to consider farm relief; I think a special session of this house should be called before the general election in England in order to see what we can do to relieve the unemployment in the old country and to adopt a real British preference. England is paying millions of dollars a day to the United States on account of the war debt, but England did the bulk of the fighting during the war and carried the financial burdens of most of the European countries as well. No one knows what England is going through to-day in an industrial way, but a rich dominion like Canada does nothing to
The Budget-Mr. Church

assist the mother country. A proper British preference which would protect British goods would d'o much in this direction.
Conditions have changed greatly in the old country during the past years. At one time England was a free trade country, the United States was a free trade country and so was Germany. The great German economist List has given a magnificent description of these countries years ago, when they all supported the free trade policy. The United States was invaded every year by an army of English commercial travellers until the great work of Horace Greeley, the founder of the New York Tribune, converted the people of the United States to protection, and to-d!ay it is the highest protected country in the world. In 1849 the Germans were so poor that they had to wear wooden shoes; that was under free trade, but later Germany adopted the principle of protection and became prosperous. The result was that in 1914 England had to ask the help of the United States to save her from the invader. We have a free trade government in Canada now; they are talking of low tariffs. At the special session of the United States congress to be held this month the question of farm relief is to be taken up, but on that question this government is a ship without a rudder; they have no farm relief policy at all. It is all very well to talk farm relief when the election is coming on, but with the Liberal party, platforms are made to get in on and not to stand on. They have no proper or adequate policy with regard to British preference and1 they will do nothing to help the Welsh miners. They even say that they have nothing to do with unemployment in Canada, that it is a matter for the provinces and the mumcipalities. The government have charge of the tariff, of trade and commerce and of the banking and immigration laws; they could make that British preference effective in two or three days if they wished to do so, but they refuse to take any action.
This is also the case in connection with empire marketing. At the Toronto exhibition the empire marketing board had a large exhibit which included some of the' articles mentioned in the budget. The British preference on those articles amounts to only five cents or one cent, and a lopsided preference such as that is no good at all; it is less than we are giving small European and South American countries. That is not the kind of British preference we want here. Welsh coal has been tried out in Canada and has been proved a superior brand of fuel, but nothing is done to further its sale in this country on a preferential basis.

In my opinion the overseas dominions are partly to blame for the condition of British industry to-day; as far as Canada is concerned, we are buying too much from the people of the United States. Loyalty in Canada seems to be largely lip loyalty, -when you get down to brass tacks. We bought more goods from the United States than England bought, with four times our population; we bought twice as much as Germany, with six times our population, and we bought twice as much as France, which has five times our population. In 1928 Canada spent $3,000,000 per day across the line, largely for clothing, boots, shoes and many other articles on this list of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), when a large part of this trade could have been carried on with the motherland. Are you content to continue this policy? If you are, then the British Empire must fail because trade follows the flag. Are you content to spend $400,000,000 to-day, when in 1896, wfith a population of only a few million less, we were spending only $36,000,000? We should give the motherland preference in our market by a real reciprocal preference tariff and not a lopsided one.
The government is doing very little for the people of the old land with its immigration policy. Immigration is related to the tariff; the two are interlocked and correlated; one cannot exist without the other and the immigration question is also related to that of the British preference. There can be no immigration as long as the present free trade panAmerican tariff policy is in force. What is the use of putting 10,000 more immigrants into the west, when there is no work for them and when you cannot market your crops properly. The grain growers of the west are suffering untold hardships, not only with regard to transportation facilities, but in an economic way. These hardships are brought about by the competition they have to meet from across the border. I might quote the great German economist List, who described England about 1840 as:
Supreme in every branch of manufacture, as a world's metropolis which supplies all nations with manufactured goods, a treasure house of all great capital, a banking establishment for all nations, which controls the circulating medium of the whole world, and by loar-s and the receipt of interest on them makes all the peoples of the earth her tributaries. In vain did the Germans humble themselves to the position of hewers of wood and drawers of water to the Britons; the latter treated them worse than a subject people.
Then we should see the United States at that same time, in 1840, invaded every year by an army of British commercial travellers. We should then have a picture of a com-

para-tive situation of the three countries at the outbreak of the war, Germany producing twice as much steel and iron as England, the United States with an even vaster production, the two countries towering in their industrial strength above the nation which had once supplied both with everything they required except food and timber. These comparative diagrams might be accompanied by others to show how national power was a reflection of industrial power, and ho.w free trade England which, as a protected country, had once ruled the world, was compelled to invoke the aid of one great protected country, the United States, to assist her in repelling the attack of another.
